—This is a guest post by Stephen Winik, a folklorist in the American Folklife Center. It also appears in the September/October issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

The American Folklife Center turns 50 in 2026, marking a half century of preserving, presenting and supporting folk culture. The celebration culminates in mid-September with the opening of a major exhibition, “Alive in Many Hands: The American Folklife Center at 50.”

The center owes its existence to the American Folklife Preservation Act of 1976. Congress charged it with safeguarding the nation’s living cultural traditions — everything from fiddle tunes and quilt patterns to holiday rituals, occupational skills and family recipes. These expressions belong to families, ethnic communities, work groups, religious congregations and regions, stretching from the mainland to the Caribbean and Pacific Islands.

Today, the center maintains one of the largest folklife archives anywhere. It exchanges knowledge and expertise with scholars and communities and produces public programs that bring these traditions to life.

“Alive in Many Hands,” part of the Library’s America 250 celebrations, pulls from the best of those collections to show how tradition thrives in countless hands across the country. The exhibit runs through early 2028.

Step into the exhibition, and the collections begin speaking.

A “crossing the line” certificate marks a rowdy rite of passage for World War II sailors crossing the equator for the first time. They were forced to perform silly tasks, subjected to teasing and trials and finally presented to King Neptune and his court — other sailors in disguise. Survivors earned the title “shellback” and a certificate to prove it.

A brick fragment from Luboml, whose Jewish inhabitants were executed en masse by the Nazis during World War II. American Folklife Center. Photo: Shawn Miller.

Nearby in the exhibit, recorded sea shanties recall an earlier age of shipboard life, when songs kept crews working in rhythm aboard sailing vessels — massive machines of wood, canvas and rope.

A few feet away sits a small wooden puzzle from Virginia’s Blue Ridge Mountains. Raymond Nichols carved its pieces with a pocketknife so that, when assembled, they nest into a perfect ball. When Nichols gave it to AFC fieldworkers in 1978, he couldn’t remember when or where he learned to cut and shape the pieces into precise dimensions. “Must have seen it somewhere when I was a boy,” he said.

A skilled woodworker, Nichols built much of his own house and furniture, including a barn raised in the traditional Blue Ridge style used by generations of farmers. A modern building inspector wasn’t impressed, though — he rejected the poplar beams and the fieldstone foundation. Nichols chuckled as he recounted the story to AFC fieldworkers: “Boys, I’ll tell you — the pioneers wouldn’t stand a chance!”

Other objects carry a heavier weight, tell stories of vanished communities.

Documentarian Candacy Taylor (left) with New Orleans chef Leah Chase, whose restaurant appeared in the Green Book . Photo: Courtesy of Candacy Taylor.

A weathered directional sign and a single brick fragment come from Luboml, a once-thriving Jewish shtetl then in Poland, now part of Ukraine.

The sign stood on a corner just outside the Jewish Ghetto — a witness to the community’s destruction. On Oct. 1, 1942, Nazis marched residents of the ghetto to that very corner, then directed them on to a place where they would be executed en masse.

AFC holds dozens of oral histories of Americans who once called Luboml home, along with thousands of pages of manuscripts and photos. Together, they preserve the memory of a Jewish community erased by the Holocaust — as does that street sign, the only one of the Nazi era known to still exist.

“Alive in Many Hands” also traces stories of struggle and progress in the United States.

Published between 1936 and 1967, The Negro Motorist Green Book guided Black travelers to safe places to eat, sleep, shop and get gas — a vital resource during the segregation era.

Through oral histories collected by documentarian Candacy Taylor and held by AFC, exhibition goers meet some of the business owners like New Orleans chefs Dooky and Leah Chase who made the book — and safe travel — possible. When segregation ended, the Green Book disappeared, but its legacy of service to the Black community remains.

A dedicated section of the exhibit explores foodways — the rich cultures and traditions surrounding food.

No matter where we live, how we work or how we spend our time, food is a constant in all our lives. We have favorite (and not-so-favorite) dishes, traditional methods of cooking and deeply ingrained customs for obtaining, preparing, eating and sharing meals.

A World War II chocolate ration. American Folklife Center. Photo: Shawn Miller.

The World War II chocolate rations, community cookbooks, military menus and mouthwatering photos of food and food preparation in the exhibit explore how food embodies our cultural traditions, shared experiences and our connections to the places we live, work and play.

Many other foodways items from the exhibit — along with compelling stories, photos and even songs about food and drink — will be featured in the forthcoming book “Sharing Food, Sharing Culture.” Part of the Library’s “Collections Close-up” series, the book is scheduled for publication in September.

Music runs through the exhibit like a living current.

Two photographs capture artists from AFC’s Homegrown concert series: Louisiana Creole accordionist Sean Ardoin and the Navajo duo Sihasin, artists who represent a long family history of music. Sean traces his lineage to legendary accordionist Amédé Ardoin, and Sihasin to community leaders, singers and dancers, including their father, Jones Benally. In their concert videos, online at loc.gov , they tell those family stories.

The photos also tell the tale of the concert series itself.

Folklorist Alan Lomax used a disc cutter like this one to record spirituals by Becky Elzy (left) and Alberta Bradford, two singers who grew up in slavery . Courtesy of E.A. McIlhenny Collection, Avery Island Archives, Avery Island, Louisiana.

Concerts have always been a part of American Folklife Center programming — the first event hosted by AFC, in February 1976, featured traditional folk music from prominent artists. When COVID shut down most social life in March 2020, AFC quickly adapted, hiring musicians to record performances wherever they could.

Sihasin, a brother and sister duo of Clayson and Jeneda Benally, performed on a windswept Arizona plain, joined by their father and their beloved horse, Moonwalker. Ardoin created a video of himself playing live with prerecorded tracks he had laid down himself. The results were powerful and intimate — and are still available on the Library’s website and the Folklife Today blog.

Technology itself gets a spotlight via a hefty Presto instantaneous disc recorder used by the Library in the 1930s and ’40s — one of a succession of technologies, from wax cylinders to reel-to-reel tapes, used to record traditional songs and stories.

The disc recorder was probably the heaviest of these technologies — and it required additional bulky equipment for playback and car batteries for power. Sometimes, the bulk and weight of these machines became part of the story.In June 1934, renowned folklorist John A. Lomax and his 19-year-old son, Alan, hauled one of these machines to Avery Island, Louisiana. The goal: record spirituals for the Library performed by Becky Elzy and Alberta Bradford — two elderly women who were born into slavery and lived through the Civil War and emancipation.

Elzy and Bradford always sang together, which presented a problem for the Lomaxes: They arrived to find that Elzy had moved 50 miles away to Lake Arthur. Drenching rains compounded the problem: The roads were deep mud, and the Lomaxes weren’t sure they could drive themselves, Bradford and the heavy equipment to Elzy without getting hopelessly stuck.

So, the elder (and heavier) Lomax stayed behind while Alan, Bradford and the equipment drove off to find Elzy. Reunited, Elzy and Bradford sang 10 spirituals, including a jubilant “Free at Last,” while Alan recorded — probably the first recordings the soon-to-be famous folklorist made without his father.

It’s awe-inspiring for anyone to hear “Thank God Almighty, I’m free at last” sung by women who suffered under slavery.

But two people were especially delighted when AFC published the recordings on the Folklife Today blog in 2019: Elzy’s great-great-granddaughter and Bradford’s great-great-grandson — neither of whom knew the recordings existed.

It’s through telling stories like this, connecting Americans to cherished aspects of our culture, that the American Folklife Center meets its mission. These are the stories you’ll find throughout “Alive in Many Hands.”

-This is a guest post by Brett Zongker and Deb Fiscella, both of the public affairs section in the Office of Communications. It also appears in slightly different form in the May/June issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

The nation’s oldest federal cultural institution is using some of the newest technology to preserve digital copies of historical collection items for the next 250 years.

As part of America’s 250th anniversary celebrations, the Library made a trailblazing contribution to America’s Time Capsule : a tiny metal pellet holding synthetic DNA encoded with digital copies of items from the Library’s collections. The capsule itself – a 900-pound stainless steel cylinder covered by a 1,100-pound stainless steel bell jar – was ceremonially buried 10 feet underground on July 4th at Independence National Historical Park in Philadelphia.

Maintained by the park and the National Park Service, it is not to be opened until July 4, 2276. Hundreds of other items – letters, memorabilia and documents, all helping tell the story of the nation’s history and culture – were all tucked in the capsule, including from all three branches of government, the Supreme Court and all states and territories. The Library’s experts helped determine which items could survive two and and a half centuries. (A bottle of Coca-Cola, an I-Phone, and the starting lineup of the Philadelphia Phillies all made the cut.)

For the Library’s tiny, data-packed cylinder, the Library initiated a molecular data storage feasibility study in response to a request from Congress in 2024. As a result, the Library has been examining the storage capabilities of a new medium, synthetic DNA. An entirely manufactured molecule, synthetic DNA is designed to replicate the exceptional information density of nature’s best storage medium: DNA itself.

Working with the University of Washington’s Molecular Information Systems Lab, the Library has converted selected digital data into synthesized DNA strands encased in a metal vial about the length of a pencil eraser.

The synthetic DNA includes, among other Library collection items, digital copies of: Thomas Jefferson’s rough draft of the Declaration of Independence; “The Star-Spangled Banner” lyrics written in Francis Scott Key’s hand; the 1791 L’Enfant plan for Washington, D.C.; digitized 1890 Native American audio recordings in Passamaquoddy; the canvas drawing of the Blackwell’s Kinfolk family tree, depicting more than 1,500 names; and the Annals of the Congress of the United States, covering congressional proceedings, including the making of the Constitution, from 1789 to 1824.

Synthetic DNA can store about nine terabytes of digital data in one cubic millimeter, approximately 1,000 to 100,000 times greater than the capacity of conventional digital storage methods like hard drives, tape drives and cloud storage. It also is highly durable, lasting thousands of years with little to no maintenance or power consumption.

The encasement includes a small chip containing decoding instructions, ensuring the synthetic DNA sequence can be reassembled into its original digital data when the time capsule is opened 250 years from now.

captures.text:
Reid Wiseman sat onstage at the National Book Festival , still marveling at the journey that brought him there.

As commander of NASA’s Artemis II mission in April, Wiseman led humanity’s first crewed voyage beyond low Earth orbit in 53 years — a nearly 10-day journey that looped around the moon and back. The deepest moments came on the far side of the moon.

“The moon is blocking our view of Earth. We can’t talk to home,” Wiseman said. “This was an amazing magical period for us, where we were truly alone in the solar system. We were further away than any human had ever been.”

The astounding view — the sun behind the moon, the moon just a black sphere pulling the spacecraft around it — was beyond the power of words to convey. “I don’t think the human mind has evolved to the point of describing what we’re looking at,” he said.

At the furthest point, the crew celebrated with maple cookies, shared a tearful group hug over a crater named for Wiseman’s late wife, Carroll, and heard a posthumous recorded greeting from Apollo 13 commander Jim Lovell: “Welcome to the neighborhood.”

And then the return home, traveling about 24,000 mph during reentry. “We’re falling straight down,” he recalled as the scene played on the main stage’s huge screens. “It was not scary inside, but it’s terrifying watching this video of what we looked like from the outside.”

Parachutes brought the spacecraft to a safe ocean landing, concluding the mission with a joyful splash. “All I’ve ever wanted to do was go see the far side. All I ever want to do is go as far away as I can,” he said.

His mission completed, Wiseman offered advice to the next generation: “For the kids, if you ever get the chance to do this, just do it.”

Wiseman came away with an enormous sense of pride in the collective accomplishment. “If you grew up in this country, if you’re an American, you should just be so dang proud of what this country could do if we tried,” he said. “This is an amazing place to live.”

– This story also appears in the July/August issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

Describe your work at the Library.

As director of the Center for Learning, Literacy and Engagement, I have the privilege of leading a team of talented colleagues who create programs and experiences that help people connect with the Library — whether they’re visiting in person, joining online or engaging from their own communities. Our work spans the offices of Library Events, Signature Programs, Informal Learning, Literary Initiatives, Visitor Engagement, and Professional Learning and Outreach Initiatives, all shaped by a deep and ongoing understanding of our audiences.

In my role, I focus on setting direction and creating the conditions for this work to thrive. That includes building consistent, audience-focused programming frameworks — like Live! At the Library, Afternoons With the Library and Family Days — that give people welcoming, predictable ways to engage. These platforms also make it easier for colleagues across the Library to bring their ideas to life and reach the audiences they care about.

How did you prepare for this position?

I’ve been working in cultural institutions for more than 35 years, which still surprises me. I began my career at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum before it opened, where I had the opportunity to play a small role in shaping the permanent exhibition and thinking about how visitors would experience it. I also earned a master’s degree in leadership in museum education from Bank Street Graduate School of Education.

I later moved to the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, where I led Education, Outreach and Visitor Experience and led the development for Q?rius, a science education center for young people.

Across these experiences, I’ve focused on ensuring that programs reflect the authentic voice of the institution — working closely with collections and experts while bringing in audience perspectives through research and advisory groups. That same approach guides my work at the Library.

What are some of your standout projects?

I’m especially proud of Live! At the Library . We had a lot of strong programming happening across the Library, but it was previously more dispersed. We created a consistent Thursday night series along with concession sales to help build a regular audience — particularly younger and working-age adults. It has grown into a weekly cultural destination averaging 850 to 1,100 attendees each week, and it has introduced many people to the Library for the first time in a way that feels welcoming and dynamic.

What have been your favorite experiences at the Library?

I’m a huge crossword puzzle nerd, and we held a Live! At the Library event with author Adrienne Raphel and New York Times crossword editor Will Shortz, who had done research with the Library’s puzzle collections. For the program, we shared some historical puzzles and Shortz created special puzzles for the audience — a great example of how the Library can bring together scholarship, creativity and public engagement in ways that feel surprising, personal and accessible.

Another especially meaningful experience has been developing The Source gallery. It’s been years in the making, with librarians across divisions helping identify collections and internal and external educators piloting and shaping how young people will engage with the space. What excites me most is seeing how kids respond — how quickly they connect with primary sources and begin to see the Library as a place for them.
paragraphs: – This story also appears in the July/August issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.
Describe your work at the Library.

As director of the Center for Learning, Literacy and Engagement, I have the privilege of leading a team of talented colleagues who create programs and experiences that help people connect with the Library — whether they’re visiting in person, joining online or engaging from their own communities. Our work spans the offices of Library Events, Signature Programs, Informal Learning, Literary Initiatives, Visitor Engagement, and Professional Learning and Outreach Initiatives, all shaped by a deep and ongoing understanding of our audiences.

In my role, I focus on setting direction and creating the conditions for this work to thrive. That includes building consistent, audience-focused programming frameworks — like Live! At the Library, Afternoons With the Library and Family Days — that give people welcoming, predictable ways to engage. These platforms also make it easier for colleagues across the Library to bring their ideas to life and reach the audiences they care about.

I also earned a master’s degree in leadership in museum education from Bank Street Graduate School of Education.

Let’s check in with 1982.

“E.T.” landed in theaters and called home. Something called “emoticons” were posted by a computer scientist and so began the creation story of emojis. CDs appeared in record stores. And the Library’s Music Division hired Raymond White, a fresh-faced young man from University of Maryland with degrees in history and vocal performance, to a permanent position.

And lo, for all the days in the world since then until the one at the very end of this month, Ray White has been a fixture at the Library of Congress. He retires at the close of business on Friday, July 31, a mere 44.5 years after he officially started. We are sorry he is leaving so soon but will wish him the best anyhow.

Ray has delighted patrons, scholars and guests of the Library with his knowledge of the field, encompassing everything from Beethoven to Broadway show tunes, including delightful asides and bon mots about great pieces of art or how simple little songs became big hits. Though he does much work behind the scenes, he is best known for his storytelling in presenting items for guests, be they students or VIPs, to marvel over.

We caught up with Ray for a final conversation recently. The following has been lightly edited for space and clarity.

What was your very first assignment at the Library?

Well, before I was hired permanently, I first started as a temporary employee in the summer of 1980. I was to sort a big pile of copyright deposit sheet music in deck 49 of the Jefferson Building in preparation for the Music Division’s move to the Madison Building, which would not occur until December of 1982. It was all quite ho-hum.

Do you still get goosebumps when special stuff comes in?

Oh, absolutely. And I still get goosebumps when I handle treasures that have been here for decades. Representatives of the Gershwin Legacy Project, founded by a cousin of George and Ira, recently visited the Library, as they’re contemplating some commemorative activities for the “An American in Paris” centenary in 2028. “Rhapsody in Blue” had its centenary two years ago. These are both works for which we have all the stuff . For “An American in Paris” we have 22 pages of George Gershwin’s autograph sketches. We have his two-piano score for the entire work. We have his short score for the whole thing and his ink holograph full score, which is right now on display in the Gershwin Gallery.

Is that Gershwin reverence ? Something else?

Part of it’s Gershwin reverence, but part of it is the recognition that we’ve got the entire documentary evidence of the creation of these works. One of the things I tell people about the Library is that we love process. We certainly want to know what the final product was, but we’re as eager to know how it got there. That’s true across the library — the Walt Whitman materials in Manuscript; you go to the Treasures Gallery and see the rough draft of the Declaration of Independence. It’s all the same principle. The rough draft is an excellent example. If the line weren’t so famous — “We hold these truths to be self-evident” — it would be far less impactful to know that Jefferson first wrote, “We hold these truths to be sacred and undeniable.”

That moment of creation … when you see the light switch on, it really humanizes it.

Yes. I also think that people who don’t handle creative drafts on a regular basis might kind of assume that these masterpieces fell down out of the sky from St. Cecilia [the patron saint of music] herself and this is how they are. But no, these are people who got up in the morning and they put on their clothes and they drank their coffee and they did what they did.

Other goosebump favorites?

I would say Bach , Beethoven and Mozart. We have two very, very fine Bach manuscripts — two of his church cantatas. Our best Beethoven is his Piano Sonata Opus 109 . And probably our best Mozart is his Violin Concerto No. 5 in A major , which, by the way, he wrote when he was 19. I’ve shown the Beethoven on several occasions to pianists who have played it and the Bach to choral directors and the Mozart to violinists. They elicit the reaction of “Oh my goodness!”

There’s a particular way you have of showing these things to people.

Well, I mean other colleagues know to do the same thing. When you’re planning for top-drawer performers coming in, you look online, you see what they’ve performed recently, you see what they’ve recorded, what might float their boat and then you see what we have. Denyce Graves Montgomery (the D.C.-born opera star) was here for a Scott Joplin event earlier this year about the Washington National Opera’s new production of Joplin’s “ Treemonisha .” We have a very rare copy of the original printed piano/vocal score of that … and we also have a printed piano/vocal score from the first production of “ Carmen .”

Which was her breakout role.

Yes. And it’s annotated throughout by the first violinist from the initial 20 performances or so with the metronome markings for “How fast does this actually go?” So, we had it on a table and her eyes got as big as saucers and she couldn’t believe it. She was just blown away and posed for pictures next to it.

Do you collect any of these types of things at home? I mean, you have the expertise from the job.

I really don’t. I have some very nice watercolors. My dining room, I have three large watercolors in Venice and they’re by artists whose names appear in the literature. But no, I really don’t collect personally.

Immediate plans for retirement? Usually, people say they’re going to travel.

My immediate plans don’t sound very exciting. I want to go home and clean my house. I want to start getting rid of things I don’t need.

Well then!

The term “travel” is kind of interesting because a lot of people speak of travel with a capital “T,” like a Nile cruise or something. My immediate travel plans are travel with a small “t,” to visit people within driving distance. I have a lot of friends. I’m very fortunate in that regard. So, I plan in the near term to do things I haven’t had time for, which might be a “have lunch with a friend” kind of thing.

captures.text:
As the 2026 FIFA World Cup gets underway, billions of fans around the world are tuning in to watch the world’s most popular sporting event. The tournament, co-hosted by the United States, Mexico and Canada, likely will be the largest and most watched in history, with over 6.5 million fans filling stadiums across all three countries, according to the Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA), the sport’s global governing body.

The 39-day tournament began on June 11 in Mexico City and concludes with the final in New Jersey on July 19. A record 48 countries are playing this year, a 50% increase from the 32 teams usually competing.

To mark the occasion, the Library’s Hispanic Reading Room is showcasing a colorful display, “For the Love of the Game,” that explain s the evolution and appeal of a sport that has become one of the world’s most influential cultural forces. The display complements a new World Cup LibGuide developed by the Library’s Latin American, Caribbean and European collections specialists.

Among the 15 items featured in the display are a rare photo album documenting the inaugural 1930 World Cup in Uruguay, memorabilia from later tournaments, a book titled “1283” about Brazilian global soccer icon Pelé — three-time World Cup champion and scorer of 1,283 goals — and another showcasing the legacy of the late Argentinian midfielder, Diego Maradona.

“When the World Cup started in 1930, it was kind of an unproven concept, but today it is clear that when you host the World Cup, you become the center of attention in the world,” said reference librarian Henry Widener, lead curator of the display . “We put together a display that explores nine decades of World Cup history and soccer’s growing popularity in American culture.”

He’s not kidding about that homegrown popularity. A 2025 survey published by The Economist found that 10 percent of Americans say soccer is their favorite sport — narrowly edging out baseball for third behind football and basketball. The U.S. is also the biggest foreign market for the four largest European leagues, according to the same survey.

Other display highlights include a newspaper image depicting Uruguay’s shocking upset of Brazil, 2-1, in the decisive game of the 1950 World Cup. And of course there’s a Panini collectible sticker album, now a tradition, that was introduced in 1970.

As any fan will happily tell you, soccer is about far more than the 90-minute drama on the field. For nearly a century, the game has helped shape national identities, triggered fierce rivalries and helped people bond over shared memories.

Widener was born in Texas and is torn between Mexico and Brazil as his pick for winning this year’s World Cup.

“As someone who has traveled a lot and talked to people from different places … if I mention the World Cup, people talk about it like it’s the most important thing in the world to them,” he said. “It really does bring people together.”

While football-like games have been played for more than 2,000 years around the world, the modern version traces its roots to England in 1863. Once the rules were codified, the game spread across trade routes and, by the time of that initial 1930 World Cup, soccer had become an international phenomenon.

The United States first hosted the World Cup in 1994, introducing millions of Americans to soccer’s four-year craze and helping to fuel the sport’s amateur and professional growth.

As fans gather in stadiums and around their TVs and watch parties over the next month, Library visitors can discover how this simple game — with its prolonged shout of “Gooooooaaal!” — became a global language.

captures.title: The Go-Go’s bring “Beauty and the Beat” to the National Recording Registry | Timeless

captures.text:
Belinda Carlisle, a child of L.A., and a couple of friends were teens hanging out in the city’s punk music scene in the late ’70s. Only one or two of them knew much about being musicians, but they threw themselves into it and by 1978, after a lineup change or two, started calling themselves The Go-Go’s.

They were, she remembers, “terrible,” but so were most of the other bands. They spent three years putting together material. No major labels were interested, so they signed with scrappy little I.R.S. Records. When they got the studio mix of their first album, “Beauty and the Beat,” they were somewhere between shocked and furious.

“We were horrified,” Carlisle, the group’s lead singer, laughed in recent interview with the Library. “It was like, ‘This isn’t us. This isn’t punk.’ I mean, I love the album, but there are songs that were sped up. I think in some songs I sound like a chipmunk.”

Charlotte Caffey, songwriter and guitarist, said Carlisle wasn’t kidding.

“We were screaming and crying and cursing like, ‘This is the worst piece of (expletive) we’ve ever heard.’ ”

Despite their horror, the 1981 album slowly but surely went to No. 1, powered by the hits “Our Lips Are Sealed” and “We Got the Beat.” The Go-Go’s, rock’s most successful all-female band, were launched into the ’80s pop-culture stratosphere of MTV, magazine covers and the national zeitgeist, headed for the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. And nearly half a century later, the album has been inducted into the 2026 class of the National Recording Registry .

There were several striking things about the album when it hit the ’80s airwaves — the energetic fusion of pop, New Wave and punk; the way the band’s sunny L.A. version of punk contrasted with the tough-guy New York and London varieties; but also, consider this: The Encyclopedia Britannica still lists “Beauty” as the only No. 1 Billboard album by an all-female rock group who wrote and performed their own material.

Caffey said that producer Richard Gottehrer’s work was a brilliant distillation of the band’s “mushy” live performances. This clarity stemmed from his background as a songwriter and producer, with ’60s credits such as “My Boyfriend’s Back,” “I Want Candy” and “Hang On Sloopy.”

“What he wanted to shine were the lyrics, the melody,” she said. “… it didn’t sound as powerful to us, but the power came through being able to hear the lyrics and to hear the song, not just this loud (onstage) craziness that we were used to. … Richard was 100 percent right.”

The band was a quintet — Carlisle, Caffey, Gina Schock, Kathy Valentine and Jane Wiedlin — and came up the hard way.

They just got up onstage, often in a tiny basement club and banged away, learning on the fly. The spot was near The Masque nightclub in the 6600 block of Hollywood Boulevard, their breakout spot. The sidewalk in front now bears their star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

The basement club, meanwhile, with is cement walls, floor and ceiling, was “ground zero for ‘Beauty and the Beat,’ ” Caffey remembers: “It was no holds barred … you know, a creative melting pot of weirdos.”

Valentine, the last member to join the group (she moved to L.A. from Austin, Texas, at 19), was a guitarist who didn’t know women could be guitarists. She’d seen Suzi Quatro fronting her own group , and it had given her an ideal. The do-it-yourself frontier of punk gave her a way to realize it. For The Go-Go’s, she played bass and wrote songs, including “Can’t Stop the World” on “Beauty” and their later hit, “Vacation.”

“The thing that appealed to me was that you didn’t have to be a virtuoso,” she said in an interview. “You didn’t have to play guitar like Jimmy Page (Led Zeppelin’s lead guitarist). You could do it right now. It’s about attitude and energy and the songs.”

The band stayed together for three albums through 1985. They went on to individual careers and have since reunited from time to time, toured, gone on hiatus, recorded together and last year played a set at Coachella with Billie Joe Armstrong of Green Day.

That show, their biggest platform in decades, was part of a series of concerts that introduced them to a new generation of fans. For Wiedlin (backing vocals, rhythm guitar, songwriting), cementing their status is a legacy project worth pursuing.

“I would like to be remembered as a powerhouse and a punk rocker and someone that broke boundaries and smashed glass ceilings,” she said in an interview. “That’d be awesome.”

It’s been half a lifetime now, but the magic of those early days in L.A. — the punk clubs, the music, the lightning-in-a-bottle energy of “Beauty” — it still resonates, both in the lives of the band and in American pop culture.

“We were at the right place at the right time with this creative energy just engulfing us,” Caffey says. “It was so spectacular.”

There were several striking things about the album when it hit the ’80s airwaves — the energetic fusion of pop, New Wave and punk; the way the band’s sunny L.A. version of punk contrasted with the tough-guy New York and London varieties; but also, consider this: The Encyclopedia Britannica still lists “Beauty” as the only No. 1 Billboard album by an all-female rock group who wrote and performed their own material.

Caffey said that producer Richard Gottehrer’s work was a brilliant distillation of the band’s “mushy” live performances. This clarity stemmed from his background as a songwriter and producer, with ’60s credits such as “My Boyfriend’s Back,” “I Want Candy” and “Hang On Sloopy.”

“What he wanted to shine were the lyrics, the melody,” she said. “… it didn’t sound as powerful to us, but the power came through being able to hear the lyrics and to hear the song, not just this loud (onstage) craziness that we were used to. … Richard was 100 percent right.”
The band was a quintet — Carlisle, Caffey, Gina Schock, Kathy Valentine and Jane Wiedlin — and came up the hard way.

They just got up onstage, often in a tiny basement club and banged away, learning on the fly. The spot was near The Masque nightclub in the 6600 block of Hollywood Boulevard, their breakout spot. The sidewalk in front now bears their star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

The basement club, meanwhile, with is cement walls, floor and ceiling, was “ground zero for ‘Beauty and the Beat,’ ” Caffey remembers: “It was no holds barred … you know, a creative melting pot of weirdos.”

Valentine, the last member to join the group (she moved to L.A. from Austin, Texas, at 19), was a guitarist who didn’t know women could be guitarists. She’d seen Suzi Quatro fronting her own group , and it had given her an ideal. The do-it-yourself frontier of punk gave her a way to realize it. For The Go-Go’s, she played bass and wrote songs, including “Can’t Stop the World” on “Beauty” and their later hit, “Vacation.”

“The thing that appealed to me was that you didn’t have to be a virtuoso,” she said in an interview. “You didn’t have to play guitar like Jimmy Page (Led Zeppelin’s lead guitarist). You could do it right now. It’s about attitude and energy and the songs.”

The band stayed together for three albums through 1985. They went on to individual careers and have since reunited from time to time, toured, gone on hiatus, recorded together and last year played a set at Coachella with Billie Joe Armstrong of Green Day.

That show, their biggest platform in decades, was part of a series of concerts that introduced them to a new generation of fans. For Wiedlin (backing vocals, rhythm guitar, songwriting), cementing their status is a legacy project worth pursuing.
“I would like to be remembered as a powerhouse and a punk rocker and someone that broke boundaries and smashed glass ceilings,” she said in an interview. “That’d be awesome.”

It’s been half a lifetime now, but the magic of those early days in L.A. — the punk clubs, the music, the lightning-in-a-bottle energy of “Beauty” — it still resonates, both in the lives of the band and in American pop culture.
“We were at the right place at the right time with this creative energy just engulfing us,” Caffey says. “It was so spectacular.”

—This is a guest post by Loras Schissel, a senior music specialist in the Music Division . It also appears in the May/June issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

It was September 1814, and British warships were unleashing a fierce bombardment on Fort McHenry, the American fortress guarding Baltimore Harbor. Rockets streaked across the night sky, shells burst in flashes of light, the city’s fate hung in the balance.

A few miles away, Francis Scott Key watched anxiously from a British ship, where he had gone to secure the release of a captured friend. Key feared the fort had fallen — until, by dawn’s light, he saw a large American flag still waving over McHenry’s ramparts.

Inspired, Key composed a poem, “Defence of Fort M‘Henry,” about what he’d witnessed — with the tune of an 18th-century British song, “ Anacreon in Heaven, ” in mind for it. Key’s creation, when set to that music, forever after would be known by another name: “ The Star-Spangled Banner. ” Though popular from its inception, it was not officially recognized as the national anthem for another 117 years, when President Herbert Hoover signed it into law on March 3, 1931.

The Library’s Music Division today stands as the principal center for research about the national anthem, thanks in large part to the visionary work of Oscar G. Sonneck.

In 1902, Librarian of Congress Herbert Putnam hired the young, New Jersey-born musicologist to establish a music department and transform it into a world-class research center. By Sonneck’s resignation in 1917, he had elevated a collection of modest parlor songs into one of the finest, most comprehensive music libraries in the world.

In 1909, Sonneck published an influential report on patriotic songs like “The Star-Spangled Banner,” “Hail Columbia,” “America” and “Yankee Doodle.” In the following years, the Library amassed a rich archive of those airs, including hundreds of items related to the national anthem.

The Music Division holds, among many other things, the first printed lyrics and the first printed sheet music of “Anacreon”; Key’s own copy of that song ; the first printed sheet music setting Key’s lyrics to “Anacreon” and bearing the title “The Star-Spangled Banner” ; and a presentation copy of the lyrics handwritten by Key years later.

A standout treasure: the first printing of Key’s poem, one of only two copies known to survive.

Typeset in Baltimore by Samuel Sands and issued as a broadside just days after Key composed his poem, this printing of “Defence of Fort M‘Henry” vividly explains the circumstances of Key’s composition and, just below, notes the intended tune: “Anacreon in Heaven.” And then: one of the most memorable opening lines in music, followed by the four full verses of “The Star-Spangled Banner.” More than a century later, a copy was found pasted in a scrapbook, then acquired by the Library.

Another treasure: An arrangement by renowned Russian composer Igor Stravinsky. At the start of World War II, Stravinsky fled Europe for America, and he created his own heartfelt arrangement of the anthem as a gesture of thanks to his new homeland.

In a letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1941, he explained: “It is a desire to do my bit in the grievous times toward fostering and preserving the spirit of patriotism in this country that inspires me to tender this my humble work to you as President of this Great Republic and to the American People.”

Stravinsky’s stately arrangement sparked controversy before it was ever heard. A leading officer of two major music organizations contacted Roosevelt, warning against Stravinsky’s “mutilated version” of the anthem. Roosevelt ignored the plea, and the first performance was presented by the Los Angeles WPA (Works Progress Administration) Symphony and a chorus. Stravinsky and the audience joined in singing the final two verses.

In 1942, Stravinsky and the WPA gifted his draft letter and manuscript to the Library, further enriching its collection of patriotic music.

It’s a charming detail that “The Star-Spangled Banner,” in its traditional form, is the only national anthem that ends in a question mark — inviting us all to keep participating in this great American experiment of democracy.

—This is a guest post by Judith Lee, the Literacy Awards program manager.

The year was 1980, and in Brazil’s teeming metropolis of Rio de Janeiro, Yvonne Bezerra de Mello started Escola Sem Portas Nem Janelas (Schools Without Doors or Windows). The idea was to offer classes on the sidewalk for kids living on the streets.

Things moved along for more than a decade. Then, in 1993, de Mello was devastated when eight of her students were among those killed by militiamen. The incident, known as the Candelária massacre, was a mass shooting by several gunmen directed at homeless teens and children living on the streets.

She dug in, though, and over the ensuing years de Mello developed her sidewalk school into Projeto Uerê, a multi-faceted program that restores learning capacity to children whose cognitive and emotional development have been disrupted by trauma.

This month, the school won the Library of Congress’ top honor in the 2026 Literacy Awards , the $150,000 David M. Rubenstein Prize , bringing the organization resources and international recognition.

“This honor represents far more than an award,” said de Mello in an interview with the Library. “It is an acknowledgment of the potential of every child to learn, grow and transform his or her future, regardless of poverty, violence or social exclusion.”

The school has worked with some 7,000 children over the past three decades, as its website explains, serving students aged 5-13 who are years behind grade level with severe learning blocks caused by trauma. The school focuses on developing each student’s attention, memory and language processing as a means of restoring basic cognitive functions.

Acting Librarian of Congress Robert Newlen recently announced the award on International Literacy Day, also naming the annual program’s other top three prize winners and 17 honorees . The groups were awarded a total of $495,000, all going to literacy-building nonprofits working around the world.

“The 2026 Literacy Awards winners and honorees have successfully demonstrated thoughtful responses to their learners’ unique circumstances in their approach to literacy education,” Newlen said.

For agencies that often work in difficult circumstances, the awards and recognition hit home.

In Grand Rapids, Michigan, Literacy Center of West Michigan received the $100,000 Kislak Family Foundation prize for their outsized impact on literacy development relative to their small size.

In New York City, Read Alliance received the $50,000 American Prize for helping K-2 students read at grade level while simultaneously providing teen tutors with meaningful paid employment, professional development and leadership training.

Finally, South Africa’s The Nal’ibali Trust received the $50,000 International Prize for distributing over 90 million reading supplements and over 116 bilingual stories to help develop a nation of young readers. The Literacy Awards had recognized the program before, in 2019, as a Best Practices Honoree.

The Library’s Literacy Awards, established in 2013 with Rubenstein’s support (and bolstered by the Kislak Family Foundation in 2023) has awarded 298 prizes, totaling more than $4.8 million. More than 240 organizations from 42 countries have been recognized for their work.

-NOTE: Our publication schedule was altered last week to accomodate reporting on the death of Dolly Parton. This piece, scheduled for last week, appears now. We knew you’d understand.

The 2026 National Book Festival arrived in style in late August, drawing tens of thousands of bibliophiles, many of whom turned up in festive shirts emblazoned with mottos such as “reading is my favorite sport,” “unreliable narrator,” “sorry, I’m booked” and “bookmarks are for quitters.”

More than 45,000 people attended this year’s event (Aug. 22) at the D.C. convention center, which showcased more than 80 authors and a pavillion full of programs featuring the Library’s collections and resources.

“The promise of a great library is that it opens doors,” said Acting Librarian of Congress Robert R. Newlen, in a short speech that opened the festival. “The Library of Congress has more doors to open than any other library in the world and we hope that you will walk through many of them. Today we have the extraordinary privilege of bringing together some of the most compelling writers and thinkers of our time with all of you, the people who love their work.”

At festival stages throughout the day, presenters spoke to the value of books and the knowledge held at the Library.

Author Tayari Jones said the event showed people continue to love reading. Fellow panelist Ann Patchett , who received the 2026 Library of Congress Prize for American Fiction at the festival, echoed her: “I’m so grateful to you for being here and for reading books.”

2025-2026 National Ambassador for Young People’s Literature Mac Barnett described exploring first editions and original printings of some of his favorite children’s books in the Library’s collections.

“It’s one of the places that kids and adults can meet as equals,” he said of children’s books.

Readers of all ages roamed the festival, including one young attendee who was so absorbed that he was walking around while keeping his nose in an open book.

On the expo floor, attendees perused an exhibit of posters from every year of the NBF — 25 from the past, plus a massive display of this year’s by Andrew Bannecker, where festivalgoers posed for photos.

Staff experts brought the Library to the convention center through a series of presentations at the Library of Congress Pavilion, as well as tables with interactive materials for guests.

Chronicling America helped kids put together zines and comics from the collection of digitized historical American newspapers. Visitors tested their knowledge with trivia from the U.S. Copyright Office, or matched books to the country of their authors with the Acquisitions and Bibliographic Access Directorate. Others practiced their librarian skills by creating authority records for their own names.

Kristen Reichenbach, a reference librarian in the Manuscript Division, highlighted the papers of Nellie Simmons Meier, a palmist who studied hands to read someone’s character. Meier collected handprints from notable contemporaries like Susan B. Anthony, Booker T. Washington and Anna May Wong, and attendees could compare their own palms with laminated facsimiles.

“It’s great for people to be able to touch history, as it were,” Reichenbach said.

The Collections Digitization Division presented at the festival for the first time this year. Among a group of collection items set to enter the public domain in 2027, visitors voted for what to digitize first by placing the item in the scanning bed and pressing a button to take a photo. (This author opted for “Dog-basket” by Diana Thorne.) All will ultimately be scanned and made available with millions of other collections online.

In the Workshop Space tucked away on the first floor of the convention center, an audience sat around tables to hear from the 2026 Academy of American Poets Laureate Fellows, offering cheers and reactions to the readings. Later in the day, the space hosted a hugely popular fiction writing workshop with novelist Angie Kim. She led participants in exercises on writing hooks, characters and voice, describing the story as the “tip of the iceberg” when it came to building the world of a novel.

The craft of writing was a theme woven across many panels by published authors.

“Your creative mind is like a friendly dog, and it brings you things,” said Elana K. Arnold, author of the young adult novel “Holloway.”

For humor writer Jenny Lawson, it’s a slow process — she said it typically takes her three to five years to write each book. Jones, the author of “Kin,” recalled returning to a spiral-bound notebook and pencil to write like she did as a kid.

“I write two sentences and then I watch 25 minutes of carpentry videos on YouTube,” said Kate McKinnon . (Relatable.)

Over the course of the 12-hour day, hundreds of volunteers in red shirts kept smiling and bringing the joy of reading to attendees.

“I’ve worked at the Library for over 10 years as an archivist and this is consistently one of the highlights of my job,” said Amanda Loeb, who served as main stage captain for this year’s festival.

captures.text:
Florence Pugh and Zoe Kazan, the star and screenwriter (respectively) of Netflix’s “East of Eden,” a fresh take on John Steinbeck’s classic 1952 California novel, recently came to the Library to get a look at some original Steinbeck material.

Among other items on display, there were signed first editions of “Eden,” manuscript pages from “The Grapes of Wrath” and a dozen or so books from the 19 th and early 20 th centuries that documented the land and the people of the Salinas Valley, the primary setting of “Eden,” “Of Mice and Men” and other Steinbeck works.

The seven-episode series, which debuts tomorrow, will stretch, like the book, from the end of the Civil War to World War I. It will also be a tale of good and evil, like the book, but is more centered around the lightning rod character of Cathy Ames, played by Pugh.

“I believe there are monsters born in the world to human parents,” Steinbeck writes in introducing Cathy in the novel, a famous sentence that also begins the series’ trailer, already viewed more than 5 million times on YouTube alone.

-This is a guest post by Josh Levy, a historian in the Manuscript Division . It also appears in the May/June issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

In June of 1876, two weeks before the nation’s centennial, a young Alexander Graham Bell arrived in Philadelphia. He was staggered by what he saw. He had come to demonstrate his inventions at the Centennial Exposition, the first world’s fair hosted on American soil, with exhibits stretched massively across more than 200 buildings in Fairmount Park. “It grows upon one,” Bell wrote his soon-to-be wife, Mabel. “It is so prodigious and so wonderful … just think of having the products of all nations condensed into a few acres of buildings.”

Like any of the era’s world’s fairs, the exhibition was a breathless celebration of progress, a spectacle of industry and commerce, art and culture. Nearly 10 million visitors attended. Those visitors may easily have passed by Bell’s telephone, but the impression of the nation’s burgeoning industrial power was unmistakable.

On the grounds stood the colossal Machinery Hall, enclosing 14 acres of exhibits and a three-story Corliss steam engine that powered every noisy machine inside. There, according to one account, one found “fire, smoke, sweat, and labor; whirring and whizzing, banging and clanging, pounding and puffing, tinkling and jingling” and machines that produced everything from “a tooth-brush to a locomotive.”

Bell’s telephone barely functioned then, and even he admitted it was still in an embryonic stage. Still, his demonstration went well. In a private showing for a small group of notables, Bell had shouted and recited and sung into the telephone from a distant room, only partially heard. At one point, after Bell asked, “Do you understand what I say,” the physicist later known as Lord Kelvin barreled toward him, announcing excitedly that he had heard the words “what I say.”

In the mythology that followed, this became a pivotal moment, the first public demonstration of a single device that broke sharply with past technology, brought forward by one brilliant inventor.

Yet real invention is seldom so straightforward. That version of the telephone’s origin is less a historical story than a legal one — a series of bold claims, made ex post facto, meant to defend a lucrative patent for Bell and his backers. “In that sense,” historian Christopher Beauchamp writes, “the invention of the telephone belongs to the lawyers.”

Samuel Morse’s brilliant success decades earlier had produced a telegraphic network bursting at the seams, and fragments of solutions to increase capacity buzzed through the air. In 1876, the telephone was still a side project, less urgent than enhancements to the telegraph system. But it was in the air as well, and soon Bell, Gray and Edison had all set their sights on improving it, with legal battles over credit and financial reward to come.

Americans have embraced stories of invention as points of national pride, from Franklin’s lightning rod to Morse’s telegraph, Bell’s telephone to the Wright Flyer.

The quiet thoughts of a lone inventor make for a good story, but the cacophony of invention as it more often happens, incrementally and in collaboration, is just as powerful, and just as American.

The drawers from the card catalog are meant to surprise you.

Open one, and a tornado from “The Wizard of Oz” swirls to life. Another reveals a rocket launch. A third shows Rosa Parks’ pancake recipe.

At The Source , the Library’s first-of-its-kind experiential research gallery for young people, the familiar wooden card catalog becomes an entry point into history, inviting visitors to explore the past not as something dusted off in a dog-eared textbook but as something they can actively discover.

Here, the past unfolds in multiple formats. Voices echo from across time, and collection items pull young visitors into the role of budding researchers. From the moment they enter the ground floor of the Jefferson Building, they can ask questions, make connections and explore history through a blend of nostalgia and modern technology.

Seven years in the making, The Source: Where Curiosity Sparks Discovery opened recently as a learning space designed to upend expectations. Created with input from 29 youth advisers and more than 40 teen interns, it reflects years of collaboration between them and Library experts. The youth advisory council met with staff over a dozen times from 2021 to 2024, shaping ideas now included across four immersive zones dedicated to collection items in text, image, sound and film formats.

For Shari Werb, lead curator of The Source and director of the Library’s Center for Learning, Literacy and Engagement, the gallery is as much about discovery as it is about skill-building. By combining curated, age-appropriate materials with intuitive digital tools, The Source allows visitors to explore and interpret content in ways that make research approachable and fun.

“We wanted to design a space that resonated with kids, so we invited them into the design process,” Werb said. “This space provides young researchers with an opportunity to follow their curiosity as they discover the primary sources at the Library.”

Unlike traditional museum exhibits, where people walk past glass-enclosed displays, The Source centers on three core ideas: engaging with primary sources, building research skills and sparking creativity. Children and teens ages 8 to 15 are invited to analyze materials, ask questions and draw their own conclusions.

That approach aligns with the Library’s broader mission. As the largest library in the world, stewarding more than 184 million items — from manuscripts and photographs to books, maps, recorded sound and film — the Library has long preserved history in its original, unadulterated form. The Source translates that mission into an experience tailored for young people, making collections accessible, engaging and relevant.

Developed as part of the Library’s long-term Visitor Experience Master Plan, with bipartisan support from Congress, The Source represents a sustained investment in expanding public access.

It also marks a shift in how research is introduced. For many young people, research can feel abstract and daunting, confined to textbooks or search engines. In the gallery, it becomes a tangible game changer: A newspaper can be scrolled on a replica microfilm reader, a photograph can be examined up close, and a single question can lead to discoveries across multiple formats.

The new learning space is, by design, self-directed and driven by curiosity, encouraging visitors to take on the role of investigators.

The welcome room sets the tone, with 30 overhead graphics reproduced from collections and 10 pull-out drawers featuring items such as “Take Me Out to the Ballgame,” Spider-Man comics and historic newspaper front pages announcing the moon landing, the March on Washington and the sinking of the Titanic, among others. The drawers, when pulled out, trigger related sounds and animations.

At its core, the gallery supports what educators call “reading to learn” rather than “learning to read.” It’s aimed at kids who already have foundational literacy skills and are ready to deepen their understanding of the world.

That philosophy undergirds the space, with high-quality reproductions that offer meaningful entry points to the Library’s holdings. Digital tools reinforce hands-on learning, allowing visitors to zoom in on details, follow prompts and develop their own interpretations. Life-sized video displays of seven librarians add a human element, as they share insights about their work and tips on navigating collections.

These tools help to demystify the research process, making it feel personal and achievable, rather than an overwhelming sensory and informational overload.

Across four zones, visitors encounter the breadth of the collections. In the text zone, 40 manuscripts and 10 newspaper front pages document historic moments, from the signing of the Declaration of Independence to the end of World War II. A replica microfilm reader shows how researchers explored such topics in the past.

In the image zone, visitors can examine more than 150 photographs, portraits, stereographs, maps and posters as they search for clues and context.

In the sound zone, drawers containing 50 recordings — from early broadcasts to oral histories, accounts from veterans and songs — can be played on a replica phonograph, giving voice to pivotal moments.

In the film zone, 59 samples of newsreels, documentaries and early clips flicker to life on a replica projector, showing how stories have been captured and shared across generations.

Threaded throughout are investigation stations featuring more than 200 curated objects, encouraging visitors to build their own interpretations.

Among the most distinctive features are research boxes — 12 completed so far — covering topics such as the Ghost Army of World War II, the evolution of basketball and research by former National Ambassador for Young People’s Literature Meg Medina into 1970s New York. These boxes let visitors follow a researcher’s journey and reach their own understanding.

Caleb Sinnwell, who joined the youth advisory group at age 14, worked on a research box about the Ghost Army, a U.S. military unit known for its use of myriad visual and audio deception tactics.

“I pushed for including a film clip that sparked my interest in the Ghost Army, which showed the unconventional methods they used to deceive Nazi forces,” Sinnwell said. “Seeing and hearing a giant speaker blasting out fake battle sounds or watching a soldier pick up and move an inflatable tank is shocking. I felt it would draw kids into the exhibit to learn more.”

Now a rising sophomore at Northwest Iowa Community College in Sheldon, Iowa, Sinnwell believes the gallery’s youth-centric approach will resonate with visitors.

“I never knew how much I loved history until I started studying and researching it using primary and secondary sources. I hope young people realize how fun and amazing researching history can be,” he added.

The educational experience extends beyond the gallery’s walls through The Source Creative Research Journal, a 48-page companion journal designed as a continuation of the visit and available for purchase in the gift shop.

Together, the 4,000-square-foot gallery, the journal and The Source website create a continuous experience from curiosity to exploration to creation.

Designed with accessibility in mind, The Source includes open-captioned videos, large-print guides and sensory kits with noise-canceling headphones and fidgets. Staff wearing Source-themed T-shirts are available to facilitate the visit.

Operating Tuesday through Saturday , the gallery can accommodate up to 188 visitors at a time and is expected to welcome about 150,000 people annually, from families to school groups. Over five years, that could mean more than 1 million young visitors engaging with primary sources — many for the first time.

At a time when information saturates the web and social media, The Source encourages the next generation of thinkers, creators and informed citizens to examine evidence and consider context to better understand an increasingly complex world.

In a place where magical card catalog drawers offer a glimpse into the past, the lesson is not just what to find but how to keep looking.

“We want kids to leave here feeling equipped — able to seek out reliable sources and think critically about what they encounter,” Werb said. “Information is everywhere, but meaning still needs a place. At The Source, young people move beyond answers to explore ideas, ask new questions and make discovery their own. In a world of instant information, this is where curiosity deepens.”

Before bestseller lists and BookTok, there was “Charlotte Temple,” an 18th-century novel that created one of America’s first and most lasting literary fandoms. By 1812, Carey wrote to Rowson that “Charlotte Temple is by far the most popular … novel ever published in this country” and estimated that the number of copies sold “must far exceed 50,000.”

In the meantime, Rowson opened a school for girls and remained dedicated to educating the young women of her “dear adopted country” until she died in 1824 — not only an American, but an American legend.

captures.text:
Ralph Ellison ’s masterpiece novel, “Invisible Man,” was greeted as a sensation in both content and style when it was first published in 1952. The surreal first-person bildungsroman tale of a young man seeking affirmation of his identity as a Black citizen in America continues to be ranked among the best works of American literature of the 20th century. Ellison became the first African American writer awarded the National Book Award for Literature when he won the prize for the novel in 1953.

“Invisible Man” is a reflection on race and humanity in an era of Jim Crow repression and Black urban migration. It charts the challenging and often-nightmarish experiences of an unnamed narrator’s physical and metaphysical travel from the American South to New York City, where he becomes deeply immersed as a witness-participant in the complex politics and cross-cultural life of Harlem. Ellison’s improvisational approach to the novel’s structure reflects his love of blues and jazz, and his incorporation of parody, puns and wordplay honor the richness of black humor and the vernacular tradition.

Ellison left school in Tuskegee, Alabama (where he studied music and read canonical literature in the library), to go to Manhattan in the mid-1930s. His employment as a folklorist with the Harlem Federal Writers’ Project and the encouragement he received from Langston Hughes and Richard Wright laid a foundation for his creation of “Invisible Man” and his long career as an essay writer and cultural critic.

The famous opening lines of the novel’s prologue (“I am an invisible man … simply because people refuse to see me”) have retained their significance into current times, and Ellison continues to inspire rising writers and readers. With “Invisible Man,” he opened a path that led to the Black Arts Movement of a following generation and spoke to existential and universal aspects of the human condition.

captures.text:
—This article also appears in the September/October issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

It was 1939, and friends gathered in the bohemian heart of Greenwich Village to toast the publication of a new book by one of their own. Frank Warner, a musician and folksong collector, arrived with a prized new possession in hand: a handmade banjo, fresh from the mountains of North Carolina.

Nathan Hicks had crafted this fretless, five-string instrument from figured walnut just months earlier, and Warner quickly customized it to his own style, adding frets and removing the drone string.

That evening, amid the good cheer and easy laughter, Warner impulsively decided on another alteration. He turned to Carl Sandburg, the famed poet, song collector and Lincoln biographer, and held out the banjo. Would you mind signing it?

Sandburg obliged, scrawling his name and the year beneath the bottom string.

The banjo Nathan Hicks crafted in 1939, now with 260 signatures. American Folklife Center. Photo: Shawn Miller.

That, as it turned out, was just the start.

Warner kept at it, collecting autographs of the era’s greatest folk musicians and scholars. Woody Guthrie, Pete Seeger, Lead Belly, Odetta, Burl Ives.

Alan Jabbour, the founding director of the Library’s American Folklife Center. Robert Gordon, John A. Lomax, Alan Lomax, Benjamin Botkin, Duncan Emrich and Joe Hickerson — each the head of what’s now the Archive of Folk Culture, part of the American Folklife Center.

Soon, the signatures circled the banjo’s body twice and climbed the neck — some 260 in all.

For the next three decades, Warner and his wife, Anne, traveled rural America, from the Appalachians to the Outer Banks, from Tidewater Virginia to New England and beyond. Together, they collected over 1,000 traditional songs and stories. Frank played the banjo wherever they went, bringing old traditions to new audiences.

Today, the American Folklife Center preserves the Warners’ vast collection of audio recordings. The signatures on his banjo form a map of the artists and traditions they documented.

In 2018, the Warners’ sons, Jeff and Gerret, donated the instrument to the center, reuniting it with the foundational recordings their parents had entrusted there years ago — a unique chronicle of American folk music’s golden age.

captures.title: An (Extremely) Fond Farewell to Dolly Parton, Library Friend and Children’s Literacy Champion | Timeless

captures.text:
Dolly Parton, the beloved country music legend and pop culture icon who died Tuesday, was also a tireless advocate for children’s literacy whose Imagination Library was given one of Library’s highest honors, part of her long association with the national library.

In the 2021 Library of Congress Literacy Awards , the Imagination Library, an initiative of Parton’s Dollywood Foundation, was awarded the David M. Rubenstein Prize of $150,000 for the program’s phenomenal national and international success.

“Dolly Parton’s work was precisely what we envisioned this prize rewarding,” Rubenstein said. “A well-run, highly dedicated literacy program that operated both with passion and a clear sense of mission. It was a privilege to know her and her work.”

The program started in Parton’s home county in rural east Tennessee in 1995 with 1,760 children under age 5 enrolled. Each child received one free book mailed to their home monthly for up to 60 months; therefore each child would have their own library when they started first grade.

By March of 2021, more than 1.8 million books were being mailed every month to children in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia and dozens of Indigenous communities across the world.

Three years earlier, Parton came to the Library to spend the day. She donated the 100 millionth copy of books shipped to children (it is now more than 330 million), sat for an interview with then-Librarian of Congress Carla Hayden and read to kids in the Great Hall. The photo of the reading, at the top of this story, is today one of the iconic images of the Library at one of its grandest and most fundamental missions — building and supporting a lifelong love of reading for all children.

“Due to our collections and their importance, we get a number of well-known people in the Library,” said Robert R. Newlen, the acting Librarian of Congress, “but when Dolly Parton came in the building that day it was like all the electricity came on at once. Her reading, and then singing, part of ‘Coat of Many Colors’ to the kids was truly special.”

The literacy work was special to Parton and her family, too, she told Hayden, particularly to her father, who was illiterate.

“My dad got to live long enough to see a lot of it come into being,” she said. “He took such pride in the fact that the little kids call me the ‘book lady.’ He was prouder of that than anything. So, it started from a true place in my heart , and it’s done so much good for so many people through the years.”

The Literacy Awards were just one of the many ways that Parton’s life and work crossed paths with the Library, some of which were highlighted in her 2020 documentary, “ The Library that Dolly Built. ”

In 2004, the Library put together an online presentation, “ Dolly Parton and the Roots of Country Music ,” that showed how her rise from tiny Sevierville, Tennessee, to worldwide stardom in the 1960s and 1970s coincided with the rise of the global popularity of country music. It includes many of her original submissions for song copyrights.

In 2014, the Literacy Awards recognized the Imagination Library with one of its Best Practices awards , recognizing the program’s efficiency and commitment to early childhood education.

And, of course, “Coat of Many Colors,” one of her signature songs, was added to the National Recording Registry in 2011. (She wrote “I Will Always Love You,” which was also inducted in 2019, as recorded by Whitney Houston.)

The 1971 guitar-and-bass ballad, sung in her tell-tale twangy earnestness, was about a painful incident when she was growing up in rural poverty in the Smoky Mountains foothills in the 1950s. The aching feeling built in her for years, she told the Library’s Cary O’Dell.

The song tells the story of how Parton’s mother took donated rags and sewed them into a patchwork coat for her. Parton loved her mother, adored the coat and proudly wore it to school — only to be ridiculed by classmates:

So with patches on my britches

And holes in both my shoes

In my coat of many colors

I hurried off to school

Just to find the others laughing

And making fun of me

My mama made for me.

“This experience had a big impact on me , so the painful part of the memory would come to the surface every now and again, then I would push it back down and then it would come around the bend once again,” she told O’Dell. “What is really remarkable about the whole journey was the fact that I carried that hurt for so long but, once I wrote the song, I felt released from the hurt. It allowed me to take something bad and turn it into a message of understanding and acceptance.”

And, as was her seemingly effortless gift, she was able to translate her specific experience in the early 1950s in a rural corner of America to a near universal understanding decades later of how to become and remain your own person, regardless of age, gender, race, sexual orientation or political affiliation.

It is difficult today to think of a more universally adored person in national life than Parton, and the reason seems clear: She wore her sincerity and decency on her sleeve, particularly her interest in children’s self-acceptance, and never backed away, modified or apologized for how straightforward she was about it.

All this could, in the 1960s and 1970s, what with her huge wigs and outré stage outfits, give the initial appearance of naivete or a lack of sophistication. It took the nation time to appreciate the depth and sincerity of who and what she was: Simply one of the great Americans of our age.

“Today,” she said in that 2016 interview with O’Dell, “lots of teachers tell me they use the song (“Coat”) to combat bullying in school because it captures the hurt. But at the same time, kids can see that you can rise above that hurt by pulling on your family, your friends, your faith and your own self-worth.”

captures.text:
Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster adaptation of “The Odyssey” introduces the epic poem attributed to Homer to a new generation of moviegoers, turning a nearly 3,000-year-old story into a fresh cultural touchstone.

The Library’s vast collections, covering centuries of time, document how artists, cartographers and translators around the world have translated and reimagined Odysseus’ journey anew. From medieval engravings to graphic novels, the Library’s holdings document how each generation seems to find fresh meaning in the mythical, decade-long struggle of the Greek hero to return home to his wife, Penelope, and son, Telemachus, following the Trojan War.

The 12,000-line prose poem originated in an oral tradition more than 2,800 years ago in ancient Greece and was performed at festivals for hundreds of years. It uses monsters, murder, war, gods and disasters to pose timeless questions about loyalty and perseverance, resilience, temptation, loss and, above all, the universal search for belonging.

The Library’s holdings on work attributed to Homer go back about 2,000 years, with a papyrus fragment from “The Iliad,” the precursor to “The Odyssey,” and then continue as the centuries go by.

Homer’s influence always seemed to be hovering, as shown in a 1597 map by Flemish cartographer Abraham Ortelius . It fuses myth and geography to trace Odysseus’ journey across the ancient world, roughly the present-day Mediterranean, in his Theatrum Orbis Terrarum.

Around this time in London, the poet and playwright George Chapman, a contemporary of William Shakespeare, had begun the first translation of “The Iliad” and “The Odyssey” into English. He began publishing installments as early as 1598.

In 1616, he published them both in “ The Whole Works of Homer, Prince of Poetts, in His Iliads and Odysses.” His vivid, poetic rendering opened the story to readers beyond the Greek-speaking world and became an enduring influence on English literature. The poet John Keats, 200 years later, was so taken with Chapman’s translation that he penned “On First Looking into Chapman’s Homer,” which itself became famous.

Then there’s the 1640 etching by Theodoor van Thulden , which captures the moment Odysseus outwits Polyphemus , the man-eating Cyclops. One of 58 illustrations in the book “ Errores Vlyssis ,” van Thulden shows Ulysses and his crew trapped inside a dimly lit cave as they get the giant drunk and drive a burning stake into its single eye before escaping.

A rare 1899 French limited edition shines a light on Princess Nausikaa , whose grace and compassion save a shipwrecked Odysseus on the island of the Phaeacians. Published by H. Piazza, it stands as a pinnacle of art nouveau art books and is the only book to be fully illustrated by the artist Gaston de Latenay. His integration of text with sweeping color lithographs, custom borders and decorative vignettes makes “Nausikaa” a highly prized rarity. The Library owns copy 80 of a limited run of 400.

In the nearly endless “inspired by” category, the Library’s Aramont Collection has three first editions of “Ulysses,” James Joyce’s 1922 novel, which took its design, inspiration and ambition from “The Odyssey.” (Ulysses is the latinized version of Odysseus.) “Ulysses” is widely regarded as the most stunning novel of the 20 th century, and its limited first edition of 1,000 copies became some of the most sought-after books of the age. (A first edition sold at auction in London 17 years ago for the equivalent today of $636,000; signed copies have sold for much more.)

The Library’s copy #361 is one of the most exceptional copies in the world.

Assembled by Joyce and a friend, it has a hand-tooled bespoke calfskin outer cover decorated with a map of Dublin, where the novel’s action takes place. Then Joyce tucked in a detailed outline that explains how the book is loosely based on “The Odyssey.” And finally, there’s a foldout, full-color anatomical schema, explaining how parts of the body relate to chapters in the book.

“What we have here is one of the most extraordinary volumes that we’ve ever come across in the past 50 years,” said John Hessler , the Library’s former curator of the Jay I. Kislak Collection (and also a “Ulysses” scholar), in an interview on the 100 th anniversary of “Ulysses.”

The impact of “The Odyssey” is worldwide, and translations held by the Library reveal hundreds of distinct voices across the ages. Polyglots will find this through the Library’s myriad translations into languages as varied Arabic, Russian and Spanish, alongside recent English translations by Emily Wilson (the basis for Nolan’s new film) and by Daniel Mendelsohn.

There’s also a unique translation into Sorbian, a West Slavic language spoken by ethnic Slavs in Germany (it’s not to be confused with Serbian). Nevila Pahumi, a reference specialist in the Latin American, Caribbean and European Division, said the Sorbian volume is a standout because it “demonstrates the Library’s commitment to collecting universally and Homer’s tremendous influence.”

Odysseus’ epic journey has come full circle in the 21 st century through graphic novels and comic books that serve as new doorways to the Homeric universe. The Library preserves this evolving medium through its Small Press Expo Collection . Within this specialized archive, Gareth Hinds’ acclaimed graphic novel adaptation uses sweeping , watercolor panels to turn ancient Greek gods and monsters into a high-impact visual landscape for contemporary readers.
